rr_clerk.text: Come in, come in. This is the anvil. Couples would clasp hands over it and a blacksmith would hit it with a hammer. Whack. That was the wedding. Cheaper than a church.
The blacksmiths were called anvil priests. They are in the village records, with all their fees.

rr_walker.text: Which side of the border am I on? I've gone back and forth five times this morning. The signs have an opinion. My boots don't.
They say a Reiver's wife would serve her man a spur on a dish when the larder was bare. That was her way of saying 'time to go and steal dinner'.

rr_historian.text: A reiver was a rider: light horse, a steel cap, a long spear and no scruples. They called a good night's raid 'Hot Trod' when the injured chased them back across the border. Good law on one side, no law on the other.
The Union of the Crowns in 1603 ended it. King James VI and I called the borders 'the Middle Shires' to stop people being so sensitive.

rr_stationman.text: There was a line here once, the Waverley Route: Edinburgh, Galashiels, Hawick, Carlisle. It closed in January 1969, to a great deal of regret.
Part of it came back in 2015. Edinburgh to Tweedbank. Not as far as Hawick, but folk live in hope.
